segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests, after holding a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council, bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the king of the Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You say so.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the chief priests were accusing him of many things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate questioned him again:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Have you no answer at all? See how many charges they are bringing against you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now at each festival he used to release for them one prisoner, the one they asked for.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was a man called Barabbas, in chains with the rebels who had committed murder in the rebellion.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The crowd came up and began to ask him to do what he usually did for them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate answered them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you want me to release for you the king of the Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he knew that it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed him over.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas for them instead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate spoke to them again:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Then what do you want me to do with the one you call the king of the Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They shouted back,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Crucify him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why? What wrong has he done?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they shouted all the more,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Crucify him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Pilate, wanting to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas for them; and after having Jesus flogged, he handed him over to be crucified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The soldiers led him away inside the palace, that is, the praetorium, and called together the whole cohort.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They dressed him in purple, and they wove a crown of thorns and set it on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they began to salute him:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Hail, king of the Jews!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They kept striking his head with a reed and spitting on him, and going down on their knees they paid him homage.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple and put his own clothes on him. Then they led him out to crucify him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They pressed into service a passerby, a certain Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought him to the place Golgotha, which translated means Place of the Skull.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They tried to give him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they crucified him and divided his clothes among themselves, casting lots for them to decide who would take what.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was the third hour when they crucified him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The inscription stating the charge against him read, “The King of the Jews.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And with him they crucified two bandits, one on his right and one on his left.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those passing by hurled insults at him, shaking their heads and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Ha! You who would destroy the sanctuary and build it in three days,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: save yourself by coming down from the cross!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way the chief priests also, along with the scribes, mocked him among themselves, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He saved others; himself he cannot save!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Let the Messiah, the king of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who were crucified with him also taunted him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the sixth hour came, darkness fell over the whole land until the ninth hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which translated means,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of the bystanders heard it and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, he is calling Elijah!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Someone ran, filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed, and offered it to him to drink, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Wait! Let us see whether Elijah comes to take him down.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed his last.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the curtain of the sanctuary was torn in two, from top to bottom.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the centurion who was standing facing him saw that he had breathed his last in this way, he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Truly this man was God’s Son!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There were also women watching from a distance, among them Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he was in Galilee they used to follow him and serve him; and there were many other women who had come up with him to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening had already come, since it was Preparation day, that is, the day before the Sabbath,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Joseph of Arimathea came, a respected member of the council, who was himself also waiting for the kingdom of God. He gathered his courage, went in to Pilate, and asked for the body of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate was amazed that he had already died, and summoning the centurion he asked him whether he had been dead for some time.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he learned it from the centurion, he granted the corpse to Joseph.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Joseph bought a linen cloth, took him down, wrapped him in the linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of rock; then he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses were watching where he was laid.

notes.note: The same Greek verb is used for what Judas does to Jesus, what the chief priests do here, and what Pilate does in verse 15. Older versions vary it as “betray” and “deliver”; this translation keeps one rendering so the chain of handings-over stays visible. The standard lexicons give “hand over” as the basic sense.

The Greek is literally “You say,” with an emphatic “you.” It can be heard as a guarded yes (“It is as you say”) or as a noncommittal reply that leaves the claim in Pilate’s mouth. Most interpreters take it as neither a denial nor a plain affirmation, and the rendering keeps that reserve.

notes.phrase: the palace, that is, the praetorium
notes.note: “Praetorium” is the Latin term for a Roman governor’s official residence and headquarters, and Mark uses it to explain a Greek word that can mean either a courtyard or a palace. Which building in Jerusalem is meant is disputed; Herod’s palace and the Antonia fortress are the usual candidates. A cohort was nominally about six hundred soldiers, though the word may be used loosely here.

The Greek verb names prostration in reverence, and what it signifies depends on who receives it. Here soldiers parody the homage owed to a king, and the kneeling is stated separately, so “paid him homage” says what the word says without the religious claim that modern “worship” carries. Many modern versions render similarly here.
Daytime hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about nine in the morning. The sixth hour (verse 33) is about noon, and the ninth hour (verses 33–34) about three in the afternoon.

The Greek word denotes someone who plunders with violence, such as a brigand or highwayman, and is distinct from the word for a thief who steals by stealth. It was also applied to insurgents, and some versions render it “rebels” here; that reading is possible but not certain. “Bandit” keeps the violence and outlawry without deciding the question.

notes.phrase: one on his right and one on his left
notes.note: Verse 28 (“And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘He was counted among the lawless’”) is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not printed in the Greek text translated here. It is generally regarded as a later addition drawn from Luke 22:37, so the numbering passes from 27 to 29.

The Greek verb is the source of English “blaspheme,” but in the first century it meant abusive or demeaning speech against anyone, not only against God. Here the abuse is jeering thrown at a man to his face, so “hurled insults at” is used. Modern versions vary among “derided,” “reviled,” and “hurled insults.”

Greek has one word for the whole temple complex with its courts and another, used here and in verse 38, for the sanctuary building itself. Most English versions render both as “temple.” This translation uses “sanctuary” so that the taunt about destroying the sanctuary and the tearing of the sanctuary’s curtain are visibly linked, as they are in Greek.

The Greek word means the anointed king Israel expected, and here it is plainly a title, set beside “the king of Israel.” “Messiah” conveys that title to a modern reader, for whom “Christ” sounds like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.
The Greek noun can mean a particular land or region, or the whole earth. Either sense is possible here, and translations are divided; “land” is chosen as the more restrained reading.

Jesus’s words are the opening line of Psalm 22, given by Mark in Aramaic and then translated. The same psalm speaks of onlookers who shake their heads in mockery and of clothing divided by lot, both echoed earlier in this chapter. The bystanders’ remark in the next verse turns on the similarity in sound between “Eloi” and the name Elijah.

The Greek has no article and can be read as “the Son of God” or “a son of God”; a Roman soldier might have meant something like “a son of a god.” Greek grammar often omits the article in this construction even when the sense is definite, and Mark’s readers would hear the title his Gospel has given Jesus from the start. “God’s Son” leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

candidates.reason: Versions split between “Sanhedrin” and “council,” and the word recurs across the Gospels and Acts, where readers should see one term for the same body.
Rendered variously as “scribes,” “teachers of the law,” or “legal experts”; it is frequent across the Synoptics and Acts, and variation would suggest different groups.

candidates.rendering: the third hour / the sixth hour / the ninth hour
candidates.reason: Numbered hours can be kept literally or converted to clock times (“nine in the morning”); the policy needs to be uniform across the Gospels and Acts.
Translators vary among “serve,” “minister to,” “provide for,” and “care for,” and the word group recurs widely with implications for how the women’s and others’ roles are read.
Rendered as “praetorium,” “governor’s headquarters,” or “palace” in different versions; it recurs in Matthew, John, Acts, and Philippians and should be handled consistently.

warnings: Verse 19: προσκυνέω is not rendered with a register form (worship; bow down before; pay homage; bow in worship) and has no register-exception note.
